extracted.intended_audience: general readers—young people, parents, and those seeking guidance on manners and character
extracted.subtask_description: Practical moral and social guidance on personal conduct (charity, courtesy, speech), gendered etiquette (men/women in public), child-rearing and discipline, ageing gracefully, and truth-telling. The page gives examples, anecdotes, and concrete behaviors to adopt or avoid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Saying no evil / avoid uncharitableness
rubrics_metrics.description: Cultivate the habit of saying no evil; guard against thinking ill of others and accustom the mind to look on the best side of persons and things.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice a mental 'guard' so you won't pass uncharitable judgments; remember 'Nobody is wholly bad.' Example: the Young Person who dismisses another as 'no good' from a prick to his vanity. Anti-pattern: quick, sweeping condemnation based on slight causes. Practicable step: when impossible to praise, say nothing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form societies or pledges to repress unkind criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Organize mutual commitments to speak kindly or remain silent when kind speech is impossible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Ten girls... formed a society for the repression of unkind criticism' and pledged to try not to speak ill and to say nothing when they could not speak kindly; initial difficulty gives way to habit of kindly speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Older people (mothers) must set an example
rubrics_metrics.description: Adults—especially mothers—should model tolerance, tact, unselfishness and charitable speech so children copy these virtues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quotation paraphrase: 'the virtues of the mothers shall occasionally be visited upon the children.' If elders show good manners, children will reproduce them; conversely, children often reflect parental faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer your seat to women — courtesy in public transit
rubrics_metrics.description: Men should give up seats in cars/omnibuses to women regardless of personal fatigue; physical differences justify courteous help.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: standing for short ride harms a woman more than a man; being a 'true gentleman' means being unselfish whether rich or poor. Example: foreign day-laborer rising is superior to millionaire hiding behind newspaper. Anti-pattern: remaining seated behind a paper while an older or delicate woman stands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reciprocate rudeness — remain courteous when others are discourteous
rubrics_metrics.description: Refusal to copy coarse or discourteous behaviour even if fellow passengers (including women) are rude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a woman giggles, whispers, or stares rudely, that does not justify your behaving like a 'rough'; do not adopt the style of a profane drunkard when forced to address him.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge courtesies — gratitude for favors
rubrics_metrics.description: When someone offers a kindness (e.g., gives up a seat), acknowledge it with thanks; acceptations-as-due are discourteous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a man rises and offers his place and the woman takes it silently, it is bad manners; nevertheless the man should persist in courteous acts even without thanks—do good for the good's sake, not for credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women should avoid loud speech and constant laughing in public
rubrics_metrics.description: A common defect in American women's public deportment is being 'loud'—talking and laughing at high volume is unbecoming.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: like a peacock—graceful until it shrieks. A woman who is 'prononcée' in conveyances or who laughs loudly and comments on fellow-passengers has no claim to be a 'lady.' Prefer soft, discreet speech in public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice small, tactful courtesies (particularly by men)
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple habitual acts—lifting the hat properly, rising when a woman enters, giving precedence in doors, picking up a dropped handkerchief—mark a gentleman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of specifics: raise hat entirely on meeting a woman; lift it when companion bows; rise when a woman enters; remain standing until she is seated; give her precedence in passing; pick up articles she drops. Their presence indicates gentlemanliness; absence marks a boor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Women: show deference to elders and avoid patronizing tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Young women should not display patronizing toleration toward older people; they must place deference to elders among their duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: youthful, foolish manners that make a young woman seem superior when conversing with older people. Expectation: blush for such behavior; cultivate humility and respect for age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid brusqueness, pertness, and sarcastic wit at others' expense
rubrics_metrics.description: Brusqueness and pertness are not wit; selecting a courteous boy as the butt of sarcastic remarks is shameful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common fault among 15–18 year-old girls; restraint and kindness are preferred to cutting sarcasm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not spoil children — consistent training is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive indulgence and fear of disagreeable scenes produce stunted, selfish characters and can harm health and longevity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences cited: delicate constitutions, early deaths, lifelong selfishness; examples: children allowed to run barefoot died of cold; undisciplined appetite causing fatal illness. Parents should consider family stock and not justify neglect by 'freedom' theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit obedience as the prime rule in training children
rubrics_metrics.description: Commands and prohibitions to children should be absolute and non-appealable so the child learns self-control and knows coaxing is useless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: certainty is less trying to children; cases cited where lack of obedience made medical treatment impossible and led to death. Training should be 'line-upon-line, protest-upon-protest' rather than laissez-faire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not delegate parental discipline wholly to servants or nurses
rubrics_metrics.description: Entrusting children to untrained or willful servants undermines discipline because the child learns the servant cannot insist on obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Result: a child becomes a 'small tyrant' conscious of no law beyond personal inclination. Parents must enforce rules themselves to prevent insubordination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early training is easier than correcting adult faults later
rubrics_metrics.description: It is far easier to train a child correctly when young than to bend a 'tough bark' and change hardened habits later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Metaphor: bending a young plant vs. tough bark of an older tree. The 'letting-alone' principle is short-sighted and cruel to the child's future prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beautify old age — keep active and refuse fear of 'getting along in years'
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not be ashamed of ageing; keep heart, soul, and body engaged; avoid artificial attempts to appear young and cultivate useful occupation and interest in others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments: maturity brings wisdom and usefulness; avoid 'pretending' youth by juvenile habits; comparison to an aging horse that still works well. Practical counsel: remain present in public life, encourage younger people, keep sympathy genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth-telling: conform to fact; verify before repeating
rubrics_metrics.description: Truth is 'conformity to fact or reality'; do not spread garbled or unverified stories—check facts before relating them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anecdote: the pneumonia/medicine story distorted by overheard fragments; danger of 'gleaning scraps' and letting imagination fill gaps. Practical rule: verify the meaning/context of overheard facts before telling them to others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration and letting the truth 'spoil a good story'
rubrics_metrics.description: Resist the temptation to embellish to excite listeners; many accounts are inflated by imagination and love of sensation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: narrators often unconsciously accept the maxim that 'it is folly to let the truth spoil a good story.' Anti-pattern: constructing 'impressionist' romances of 'splash and glare' that distort symmetry and right coloring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not confuse frankness with truthfulness — avoid gratuitous, unkind candor
rubrics_metrics.description: Being 'too frank'—utterly candid about another's faults—is not true honesty but impertinence if it inflicts unnecessary pain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: blunt criticisms about dress, household management, or appearance are unwarrantable liberties. One may be truthful without bestowing gratuitous advice; needless frankness often stems from disagreeable temper rather than principle.
